nameStory: The 'groundcherry' name comes from this plant's unusual habit of dropping its papery-wrapped fruits right onto the ground when ripe, like little lanterns that have fallen from the sky. The 'long-leaved' part distinguishes it from its shorter-leaved cousins, though at 1-3 inches long, the leaves aren't exactly giant by plant standards!
description: Long-leaved groundcherry is a knee-high perennial herb that looks like a small, wild cousin of tomatoes and peppers. Growing 8-24 inches tall, it produces cheerful yellow flowers with dark purple centers that develop into small berries wrapped in papery, balloon-like husks. The plant has a somewhat sprawling growth habit with oval leaves that feel slightly fuzzy to the touch.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: The berry sits inside a papery, inflated husk up to 1.4 inches long with ten distinct veins running from tip to base - like a tiny Chinese lantern with clearly marked ribs

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bell-shaped yellow flowers up to 3/4 inch wide with distinctive dark purple or brownish markings around the center, blooming one at a time where leaves meet the stem

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval-shaped leaves 1.5-3 inches long with a slightly fuzzy texture, arranged alternately on stems and attached by short leaf stalks

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing perennial herb reaching 8-24 inches tall with a somewhat sprawling, branching pattern that spreads from underground rhizomes

habitat: Look for long-leaved groundcherry in disturbed soils, field edges, roadsides, and waste places throughout New England. It prefers well-drained, sandy or gravelly soils and full to partial sun, often appearing in areas that have been recently cleared or cultivated.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge from underground rhizomes as soil warms, with young leaves appearing fuzzy and light green.
seasonality.summer: Yellow flowers with purple centers bloom from June through August, followed by the development of distinctive papery husks around developing berries.
seasonality.fall: Ripe berries drop to the ground still wrapped in their tan, papery husks, while above-ground plant parts begin to yellow and die back.
seasonality.winter: Only underground rhizomes survive, with dried stem remnants and scattered papery husks sometimes visible on the ground.

funFact: Despite being in the nightshade family alongside deadly nightshade and jimsonweed, the ripe berries of groundcherries are perfectly edible and taste like a cross between a tomato and a pineapple - they're even sold as gourmet 'husk cherries' in fancy grocery stores!
confusionNotes: Other groundcherry species look very similar, but long-leaved groundcherry's papery husk has exactly ten distinct veins running lengthwise - count the ribs like you're examining a tiny umbrella frame. The clammy groundcherry feels stickier to touch, while hairy groundcherry is much more densely fuzzy all over.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the 'cherry' name fool you - groundcherries aren't related to true cherries at all, but are actually cousins of tomatoes, potatoes, and peppers in the nightshade family. The name comes purely from the small, round, cherry-sized fruits.
compareHints: Long-leaved groundcherry has the longest papery husks among New England's groundcherries, reaching up to 1.4 inches with ten clear veins. Clammy groundcherry feels sticky and has shorter, rounder husks, while hairy groundcherry is covered in dense, soft hairs that make it feel almost velvety compared to long-leaved groundcherry's light fuzziness.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's groundcherries, clammy groundcherry stands out for its distinctly sticky texture – other species like hairy groundcherry are fuzzy but not sticky, while strawberry groundcherry tends to be more smooth.
Among New England's groundcherries, strawberry groundcherry stands out for its distinctly fuzzy, gray-green appearance created by dense soft hairs.
Large-flowered tomatillo differs from other New England groundcherries by having the largest flowers (3/4 inch across) and fruits that nearly fill their husks.
Cape gooseberry stands out from other New England groundcherries by its larger size, distinctly heart-shaped leaves, and bigger, more golden fruits.
Among New England's groundcherries, hairy groundcherry stands out for its exceptionally fuzzy, glandular stems and leaves that feel almost velvety.
